title: Angle of an Interior Court at Angkor Wat
location_name: Angkor Wat, Siem Reap Province, Cambodia
historical_record: Emile Gsell made this albumen print in 1866 while accompanying Doudart de Lagree at the beginning of the Mekong Exploration Commission's photographic survey of Angkor. The Metropolitan Museum of Art identifies the scene as a corner of a court within Angkor Wat, the vast twelfth-century Khmer temple conceived as an earthly image of Mount Meru. Gsell's photographs became some of the earliest systematic photographic records of the monument and show its architecture before later conservation campaigns.
source: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, object 286880; Emile Gsell, albumen silver print from glass negative
rights: Public domain under The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access policy; the museum object page and API mark the image as public domain.
date_evidence: The Metropolitan Museum of Art collection record dates Gsell's photograph to the exact year 1866 and describes the 1866 expedition on which the photographic survey began.
location_evidence: The Met identifies the view as a corner of a court within Angkor Wat. The pin is the mapped Angkor Wat temple complex, OSM way 1113380295, rather than the broader Angkor archaeological zone.
image_evidence: The direct Met image is the primary Open Access image associated with object 286880 and matches the museum's title, photographer, medium, and view of the interior court.

title: Medinet Habu
historical_record: John Beasley Greene, one of the earliest photographer-archaeologists to work in Egypt, made this salted-paper print at Medinet Habu in 1854. The Metropolitan Museum of Art identifies the scene as a corner of the second courtyard of the mortuary temple of Ramesses III, including an inscription recounting the king's victories in year five of his reign. Greene's image joins archaeological documentation to a deliberately shadowed composition, recording ancient writing and architecture at a formative moment in the history of field photography.
source: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, object 266121; John Beasley Greene, salted paper print from paper negative
rights: Public domain under The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access policy; the museum object page and API mark the image as public domain.
date_evidence: The Metropolitan Museum of Art collection record gives the photograph's exact date as 1854 and places Greene's Egyptian archaeological work between 1852 and 1855.
location_evidence: The museum title and curatorial text explicitly identify Medinet Habu and the temple's second courtyard. The pin is the mapped mortuary-temple complex, OSM way 89828345.
image_evidence: The direct Met image is the primary Open Access image for object 266121 and depicts the inscribed court wall described in the museum record.

title: The Court of Lions in the Alhambra
location_name: Court of the Lions, Alhambra, Granada, Spain
historical_record: John Gregory Crace's 1855 albumen photograph records the Court of the Lions at the Alhambra during the first decades of architectural photography. Built under the Nasrid ruler Muhammad V in the later fourteenth century, the court brings together carved stucco, slender columns, and a hydraulic system centered on the celebrated fountain. The photograph helped make the palace available for close study beyond Granada while preserving a view of the court before modern restoration campaigns.
source: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, object 270824; John Gregory Crace, albumen silver print
rights: Public domain under The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access policy; the museum object page and API mark the image as public domain.
date_evidence: The Metropolitan Museum of Art collection record assigns the photograph the exact year 1855, with no circa or range qualifier.
location_evidence: The museum title explicitly names the Court of Lions, and the Alhambra's official site identifies the same court and fountain. The pin is the mapped courtyard, OSM way 92528628.
image_evidence: The direct Met image is the primary Open Access image for object 270824 and matches the full Court of Lions composition catalogued as plate 10.

title: Metropolitan Cathedral of Mexico City
location_name: Mexico City Metropolitan Cathedral, Mexico City, Mexico
historical_record: Published in 1919, this Keystone View Company stereograph presents the Metropolitan Cathedral on the north side of Mexico City's main square. The cathedral was constructed in successive campaigns from the sixteenth into the nineteenth century, so its Renaissance, Baroque, and Neoclassical elements embody several phases of colonial and postcolonial urban history. As a mass-circulated stereograph, the image also shows how monumental architecture was packaged for international visual travel in the early twentieth century.
source: Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division, item 2021636274; Keystone View Company stereograph
rights: No known restrictions on publication, according to the Library of Congress Rights Advisory for the item.

location_evidence: The Library of Congress title explicitly identifies the Mexico City cathedral. The pin is the mapped cathedral footprint on the north side of the Zocalo, OSM way 862873648.
image_evidence: The image URL is the Library of Congress large JPEG generated from the original and is listed in the item record as digital file stereo.1s32865.

title: Golden Gate Bridge from the Southwest
location_name: Golden Gate Bridge, San Francisco, California, United States
historical_record: This photograph was made on 3 September 1937, only months after the Golden Gate Bridge opened to pedestrians on 27 May and to vehicles the following day. The suspension bridge joined San Francisco to Marin County across a strait long considered difficult to bridge because of its depth, currents, winds, and fog. Its long main span, steel towers, and International Orange finish quickly transformed an immense engineering project into one of the most recognizable constructed landscapes of the twentieth century.
source: Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division, item 90707017; photographic print dated 3 September 1937
rights: No known restrictions on publication, according to the Library of Congress Rights Advisory for the item.

location_evidence: The Library of Congress title identifies the Golden Gate Bridge and the southwest viewpoint. The pin is the mapped bridge structure, OSM way 370672707.
image_evidence: The direct Library of Congress JPEG is the digital reproduction cph.3b46162 attached to item 90707017 and shows the complete southwest bridge view.

title: Rain, Steam, and Speed - The Great Western Railway
location_name: Maidenhead Railway Bridge, Taplow, United Kingdom
historical_record: J. M. W. Turner exhibited this painting in 1844, placing a steam locomotive on Isambard Kingdom Brunel's Maidenhead Railway Bridge amid rain and vapor. The National Gallery identifies the view as looking east toward London while the train travels west, with the older road bridge visible to the left. Made during Britain's railway boom, the work treats modern engineering as a subject for ambitious landscape painting and sets mechanical speed against the river, weather, agriculture, and a tiny running hare.
source: The National Gallery, London, NG538; J. M. W. Turner, oil on canvas
rights: The underlying artwork is public domain; the displayed faithful reproduction is identified as public domain on Wikimedia Commons.

location_evidence: The National Gallery explicitly identifies Brunel's Maidenhead Railway Bridge and the eastward view; Historic England independently documents the listed bridge. The pin is OSM way 511816111.
image_evidence: The displayed file is a full public-domain reproduction identified on Wikimedia Commons as the National Gallery painting NG538, matching the official title and composition.

title: Meguro Drum Bridge and Sunset Hill
location_name: Former Drum Bridge site, Meguro River, Tokyo, Japan
historical_record: Utagawa Hiroshige designed this winter view in 1857 for the series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo. The Cleveland Museum of Art identifies the arched stone span across the Meguro River as the Drum Bridge, named for its rounded profile, with Sunset Hill rising beyond it and snow-covered travelers crossing below. The print preserves a specific piece of Edo's suburban topography, including the nearby sweet-shop roof, while turning an engineered river crossing into a study of weather and movement.
source: Cleveland Museum of Art, object 1924.971; Utagawa Hiroshige, color woodblock print

image_evidence: The direct Cleveland Open Access print JPEG belongs to object 1924.971 and reproduces the full vertical sheet catalogued by the museum.

title: Minerva Terrace, Yellowstone
location_name: Minerva Terrace, Mammoth Hot Springs, Yellowstone National Park, United States
historical_record: Thomas Moran painted this watercolor in 1872 after joining Ferdinand V. Hayden's 1871 survey of the Yellowstone region. Working alongside photographer William Henry Jackson, Moran helped produce visual evidence of geothermal landscapes that circulated in Washington as Congress considered protecting Yellowstone. The National Gallery of Art treats these watercolors as both historical documents and works of art; Congress established Yellowstone as the world's first national park in March 1872.
source: National Gallery of Art, object 156720; Thomas Moran, watercolor over graphite on paper
rights: CC0 / public domain. The National Gallery of Art marks the media as free and public domain, and the displayed Commons file is labeled CC0.
date_evidence: The National Gallery of Art object record dates Moran's watercolor to the exact year 1872.
location_evidence: The National Gallery title names Minerva Terrace, and the National Park Service lower-terraces guide identifies Minerva Spring and Terrace within Mammoth Hot Springs. The pin is OSM way 837190314.
image_evidence: The Wikimedia Commons file is the NGA Open Access image for object 156720, identified by title, artist, year, and accession number and licensed CC0.

title: Columns of the Temple of Neptune at Paestum
location_name: Temple of Hera II (Temple of Neptune), Paestum, Italy
historical_record: Constantin Hansen painted this architectural study during a documented visit to Paestum in June 1838. Standing inside the building traditionally called the Temple of Neptune, now generally identified as the second Temple of Hera, he used its massive Doric columns to frame the more distant Temple of Athena. Hansen had trained as an architect before becoming a painter, and the work turns careful observation of an ancient Greek sanctuary into a precisely structured record of scale, light, and surviving masonry.
source: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, object 438949; Constantin Hansen, oil on canvas
rights: Public domain under The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access policy; the museum object page and API mark the image as public domain.
date_evidence: The Metropolitan Museum of Art dates the painting to the exact year 1838 and specifies Hansen's visit to Paestum in June of that year.
location_evidence: The Met states that Hansen stood within the so-called Temple of Neptune at Paestum and framed the Temple of Athena beyond its columns. The pin is the mapped temple footprint, OSM way 255691054.
image_evidence: The direct Met image is the primary Open Access image for object 438949 and reproduces the complete painting described by the museum.

title: El Deir, Petra
historical_record: David Roberts made this 1839 color lithograph of Ad Deir, the monumental rock-cut facade high above Petra's central valley. The Cleveland Museum of Art catalogues the sheet as El Deir Petra, while UNESCO identifies the Monastery as part of Petra's exceptional fusion of Hellenistic architectural forms with Nabataean rock-cut traditions. Roberts's widely circulated images helped establish Petra in nineteenth-century European visual culture, though their staged figures and color also remind viewers that these were composed works, not neutral records.
source: Cleveland Museum of Art, object 1927.141; David Roberts, color lithograph
rights: CC0 under the Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access Initiative; the museum permits free reuse of the image and metadata.
date_evidence: The Cleveland Museum of Art collection page and Open Access API date Roberts's lithograph to the exact year 1839.
location_evidence: The museum title identifies El Deir at Petra, and UNESCO independently names the Deir or Monastery among Petra's principal rock-cut monuments. The pin is the mapped facade, OSM way 41032088.
image_evidence: The direct Cleveland print JPEG belongs to object 1927.141 and reproduces the complete Open Access color lithograph catalogued as El Deir Petra.
